## The big idea

Drag has exactly two ingredients: **friction** (shear on the skin — the
boundary layer's bill) and **form** (pressure imbalance from a wake —
what separation costs). Blunt bodies pay mostly form drag; streamlined
ones mostly friction. The currency of the whole trade is
$C_D$ — and for engineers, the product $C_D A$, which is the number you
actually buy and sell.

::: {.callout-note}
### The numbers in charge: C_D and Re
$F_D = C_D \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 A$. But $C_D$ itself answers to Re — and
for rounded bodies it does something spectacular at Re ≈ 3×10⁵ that
explains golf balls, and a baseball pitch that flutters.
:::

## Where drag comes from

Friction drag you can already price: it's the boundary-layer shear of
7.1, integrated over the wetted skin — `CF_flat_plate` and
`plate_drag` do the arithmetic. Form drag needs the 6.2 story one more
time. Flow accelerating around a body's front face enjoys a favorable
pressure gradient; past the widest point it must *decelerate* against an
adverse one — and the near-wall fluid, already tired, gives up: zero wall
shear, then reversal, then **separation**. Behind the separation line
sits a broad, churning wake at roughly the low pressure of the shoulder —
while the nose still bears full stagnation pressure. That fore–aft
pressure imbalance *is* form drag, and for blunt bodies it dwarfs
friction. (Your homework already measured this once: the cylinder
problem, where honest flat-plate arithmetic pinned skin friction at ~14%
of the total — the wake owned the rest.)

So the design lesson inverts intuition: **the back matters more than the
front.** A blunt nose costs little (the flow negotiates it); a blunt tail
costs everything (the flow abandons it). Hence the teardrop: its long,
gentle tail exists to keep the adverse gradient mild enough that the
boundary layer never quits. Streamlining is separation management.

## The drag crisis, and the pitch that weaponizes it

For spheres and cylinders, $C_D$ holds near 0.4–0.5 across a huge Re
range — then, near $\mathrm{Re} \approx 3\times10^5$, it **collapses** by
a factor of ~4. The mechanism is pure 7.1: the boundary layer transitions
to turbulent *before* separating, the turbulent layer's imported momentum
lets it cling farther around the back, the wake narrows, form drag
plummets. Roughness triggers transition early — which is why golf balls
are dimpled *on purpose*: a dimpled ball buys its drag crisis at driving
speeds and flies far beyond any smooth ball.

Now the case study your instructor loves: **the knuckleball.** A baseball
(d ≈ 7.4 cm) at ~30 m/s sits at Re ≈ 1.5×10⁵ — parked *just below* the
smooth-sphere crisis, in the zone where a little roughness decides
everything. Thrown with almost no spin, the ball's raised seams act as
trip strips — but asymmetrically: wherever a seam happens to sit, that
side's boundary layer goes turbulent and separates late, the other side
separates early, and the lopsided wake pushes the ball *sideways*. As the
ball drifts through its half-rotation, the seam geometry slowly changes
and the side force wanders with it: the flutter that makes catchers wear
the big glove. One pitch, powered entirely by this module.

```{ojs}

viewof V_72 = Inputs.range([5, 45], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "ball speed (m/s)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - V_72
rho_a, mu_a, d_ball = 1.204, 1.81e-5, 0.074
Re_ball = rho_a*V_72*d_ball/mu_a
Res = np.logspace(1, 6.6, 400)
Cds = [cd_sphere(R_) for R_ in Res]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.loglog(Res, Cds, lw=2.5)
ax.axvspan(1.5e5, 4e5, color='orange', alpha=0.18)
ax.annotate('the crisis zone:\nroughness decides', (1.7e5, 0.9), fontsize=9, color='darkorange')
ax.plot(Re_ball, cd_sphere(Re_ball), 'o', ms=12, mfc='gold', mec='k', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f'  baseball @ {V_72} m/s\n  Re = {Re_ball:,.0f}', (Re_ball, cd_sphere(Re_ball)*1.25), fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel('Re'); ax.set_ylabel('C_D (smooth sphere)')
ax.grid(which='both', alpha=0.25)
ax.set_title("the smooth-sphere curve — seams and dimples move the cliff to the left")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Slide through pitching speeds: the ball rides the cliff's edge, which is
precisely why seam orientation — a few millimeters of stitching — can
command the trajectory. Dimples, seams, fuzz (tennis), and surface prep
are all one technology: *scheduling the crisis*.

## Drag build-up: pricing a whole machine

Industry's estimating method predates CFD and outlives it: decompose the
machine into parts, assign each a $C_D$ and area from data
(`CD_SHAPES`), and sum the drag *areas* — because $C_D A$, not $C_D$, is
what nature bills:

```{pyodide}
rider = DragBuildup(rho=1.204, name="commuter cyclist, 30 km/h")
rider.add('rider, upright', Cd=1.10, A=0.55)
rider.add('bike frame + wheels', Cd=0.90, A=0.10)
rider.add('panniers', Cd=1.00, A=0.08)
rider.report(V=30/3.6)
```

Edit it: tuck the rider (`cyclist_racing_tuck`, A ≈ 0.36), ditch the
panniers, re-run. The report's percentage column is the design agenda in
one glance — and the reason time-trialists obsess over posture rather
than frame paint. Homework applies the same bookkeeping to a semi-truck
fairing retrofit, where the percentages become dollars.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
Streamlining is not a pointy front. Sharpening the nose of a blunt body
barely helps; *tapering the tail* is what shrinks the wake — and a
truncated teardrop beats a spear every time. (Corollary with a safety
edge: a car's drag story is written behind the rear window, which is why
vortex generators and spoilers live *there*.)
:::


½ρU²·C_dA, then ×U for power: the drag trilogy. Every vehicle spec sheet is negotiating with it.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** At highway speed, roughly what fraction of a modern sedan's engine power fights drag, and how does that fraction change at double the speed?</summary>
Drag power scales as $U^3$ (force ∝ U², times U). If drag takes ~60% of
power at 100 km/h, doubling speed multiplies drag power by 8 — which is
why top speed is an exercise in diminishing returns and why EVs quote
range at specific speeds.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** A smooth ball and a dimpled ball, same size, both at Re = 2×10⁵. Which has *less* drag, and what did the dimples do mechanically?</summary>
The dimpled ball — its tripped, turbulent boundary layer hugs the surface
farther around the back, narrowing the wake. Dimples *raise* skin
friction slightly and *slash* form drag: a trade blunt bodies win big.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Why does a knuckleball flutter while a fastball (rapid backspin) curves *steadily*?</summary>
The fastball's spin averages the seam geometry over many rotations per
flight — its wake asymmetry is steady (that's Magnus lift, next module).
The knuckleball's near-zero spin lets the seam pattern — hence the
separation asymmetry, hence the side force — evolve *slowly and
unpredictably* during flight. Steadiness comes from spin.
</details>
